title: The sick (Rule 36)
hookLine: care for the sick above all, as if serving Christ
tomorrow: can being on fire for God ever go sour?

cards: A hospital waiting room keeps its own clock. The vending machine hums, a TV plays to nobody, a family checks their phones for news. Whatever was on the calendar this week just stopped, and nobody argues with that.
Benedict's monastery runs on a careful clock too: prayer at set hours, work, meals, silence. So who gets to break the schedule? Chapter thirty-six of his Rule answers in its first breath.
Before all things, and above all things: the sick. Not the prayers first. Not the work.
The people who can't keep the rhythm go to the front of the line.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.
teach.b: His reason comes straight from the Gospel. Serve the sick as Christ himself, Benedict says, because Christ said in Matthew: "I was sick, and ye visited me."
And: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Then he gets practical.

teach.h: A ROOM, AN ATTENDANT, A BATH.
teach.b: The sick get a room of their own, and an attendant who is careful and God-fearing. They get baths as often as it helps them, and the very weak may eat the meat the healthy monks go without.
The abbot's great care is that the sick are never neglected. Then a line in the other direction, and it's very human.

The sick should remember they're served for God's honor, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands. And even when they do, they're to be borne with patiently. Nobody in this chapter is a saint on a poster.
There's a tired attendant, a demanding patient, an abbot who has to keep checking. Here's the one to tell a friend: in a house built on a schedule, the people who can't keep the schedule go first.
Benedict looks at an ordinary sickroom, with its smells and its complaints, and says: Christ is here.

how: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members at home in the monastery, and the Rule's chapter on the sick is read as part of the Rule in community.

o: the people Benedict says to serve first, as Christ
monks too weak to keep the schedule, sent home
patients in a hospital the monastery ran

p: I was sick, and ye visited me
may eat the meat others skip

s: for Benedict, caring for the sick is one good deed among many
the easy reading. his chapter opens: before all things and above all things.
Benedict says the sick shouldn't burden others with unreasonable demands
and yet, even when they do, they're to be borne with patiently.
Benedict's sick monks kept the same food and schedule as everyone else
they had their own room, baths as needed, and meat for the very weak.

games.q: you're running the group project schedule. one member is out sick and still wants to help. what does Benedict's chapter point to?
o: drop him from the group; he can't keep the schedule.
make him keep up; the sick shouldn't burden anyone.
give him a light part, and keep checking on him.
games.why: the sick go before all things, and the abbot keeps checking so no one is neglected. the 'no demands' line is for the patient, not a reason to push him.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is ill right now, near or far. Write them a short message on your phone, one or two lines, nothing to fix, just that they're at the front of your line today.
Send it whenever it feels right, and for the rest of the sit, simply hold their face.

wordCard.voice: The sick. In Benedict's Rule, the people served before all things, as if serving Christ, with patience on both sides.

orig.note: Latin for the sick, the weak: Benedict's chapter is on the sick brothers.

carryVoice: The line for today: before all things, the sick, even in a house that runs on order. Rest well.
